topics.t: Tenali Raman-style wit: reading a clever tale
topics.h: What wins in a king's court when there is no sword in your hand? A sharp mind and a quick, kind reply!
p: The lesson 'The Wit that Won Hearts' is about how clever, good-humoured thinking can win people over.
Tenali Raman (Tenali Ramakrishna) was a poet in the court of King Krishnadevaraya of the Vijayanagara Empire in the 16th century. Folk tales about his clever answers are told all over India.
Wit is the ability to think quickly and say something clever and amusing. A witty person solves a problem with words and ideas, not with force.
Most wit tales follow a pattern: a tricky challenge, a clever plan or reply, and a surprising ending that makes people laugh and learn.
Wit wins hearts when it is kind: it makes a point and makes people smile without hurting anyone.

ex.q: Read: A proud merchant told the court, "I can sell anything, even air!" Tenali handed him an empty jar. "Then sell me this jar of fresh Vijayanagara breeze for one gold coin." The merchant peeped in and said, "But it is empty!" "Exactly," said Tenali, "and so was your boast." The whole court laughed, even the merchant. Think it through: what made Tenali's reply witty?
st: The merchant made a big boast: he could sell anything, even air.
Tenali turned the boast into a test by offering a jar of 'air'.
When the merchant called the jar empty, Tenali said the boast was empty too.
The reply was quick and funny, and it made its point without being cruel, so even the merchant laughed.
ex.a: Tenali used the merchant's own words against him in a quick, funny way, showing that the boast had nothing behind it.

topics.rl: When a friend teases you and you answer with a friendly comeback that makes everyone laugh, including your friend, that is wit in action.

rv.summary: 'The Wit that Won Hearts' shows how clever, good-humoured thinking can win people over, like Tenali Raman in King Krishnadevaraya's court. Kind wit solves problems with words, not force, and hurts no one.
focus: Explain what makes a reply witty in a short tale.
Know the pattern of a wit tale: challenge, clever plan or reply, surprising ending.
Recall that Tenali Raman was a poet in Krishnadevaraya's court (Vijayanagara Empire).
remember: Wit is the ability to think quickly and say something clever and amusing.
Wit tale pattern: a tricky challenge, a clever plan or reply, and a surprising ending.
Wit wins hearts when it is kind: it makes a point and makes people smile without hurting anyone.
traps: Don't mix up Tenali Raman (Krishnadevaraya) with Birbal (Akbar).
A joke that hurts someone is not kind wit.
Don't take a witty reply literally; look for the comparison, like the empty jar and the empty boast.

topics.t: Humour: idioms and funny expressions
topics.h: If your friend says she is 'pulling your leg', should you check your leg? No! Welcome to the funny world of idioms.
p: Humour is the quality that makes something funny. 'Humour' is the British and Indian spelling; 'humor' is American. The adjective is 'humorous' in both, with no 'u' after the first 'o'.
Humour often comes from surprise, exaggeration (saying something is much bigger than it is) and funny misunderstandings.
An idiom is a group of words whose meaning is different from the meanings of the separate words. 'Pulling my leg' means teasing me, not tugging my leg.

Useful humour idioms: crack a joke (tell a joke), in stitches (laughing a lot), keep a straight face (not laugh), tickled pink (very pleased), have the last laugh (win in the end after being doubted).

ex.q: Think it through: Priya told Arjun, "Exams are cancelled forever!" Arjun's face lit up. Priya grinned, "I'm just pulling your leg!" What does Priya mean?
st: Look at the idiom: 'pulling your leg'.
Nobody's leg is actually being pulled, so it is not literal.
Priya grinned after saying something too good to be true.
So the idiom means she was teasing or joking.
ex.a: Priya was joking; exams are not really cancelled.

topics.rl: Comedy shows, cartoons and the jokes your grandparents tell at family dinners are full of exaggeration and idioms.

rv.summary: Humour often comes from surprise, exaggeration and funny misunderstandings. Idioms have meanings different from their separate words, like 'pulling my leg', which means teasing.
focus: Know the meanings of humour idioms.
Spell 'humour' (British and Indian) and 'humorous' correctly.
Spot exaggeration used to be funny.
remember: An idiom is a group of words whose meaning is different from the meanings of the separate words.
crack a joke (tell a joke), in stitches (laughing a lot), keep a straight face (not laugh), tickled pink (very pleased), have the last laugh (win in the end after being doubted).
'Humour' is the British and Indian spelling; 'humor' is American. The adjective is 'humorous'.
traps: Don't take an idiom literally: 'in stitches' is not about sewing.
Don't keep the 'u' in the adjective: write 'humorous', not 'humourous'.

topics.t: Reported speech: telling what someone said
topics.h: The king said something clever at dinner, and now the whole palace wants to know. How do you pass it on without quoting every word?
p: Direct speech gives the speaker's exact words inside quotation marks: Tenali said, "I am ready."
Reported (indirect) speech gives the meaning without quotation marks, often with 'that': Tenali said that he was ready.
When the reporting verb is in the past (said, asked, told), the tense usually moves one step back: am/is → was, are → were, will → would, can → could, simple past → past perfect.
Pronouns and words of time and place change: I → he/she, today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, yesterday → the day before, here → there, now → then, this → that.
Questions use 'asked' with if/whether (yes/no questions) or the wh-word, in normal statement order: The king asked where Tenali was going. Commands use told/ordered + to: The king told him to sit.

ex.q: Change to reported speech: The king said, "I will reward the wisest man tomorrow."
st: The reporting verb 'said' is in the past, so the tense moves back: will → would.
The pronoun changes: I → he (the king).
The time word changes: tomorrow → the next day.
Remove the quotation marks and add 'that'.
ex.a: The king said that he would reward the wisest man the next day.

topics.rl: News reporters use reported speech all the time: 'The minister said that the bridge would open soon.' You use it too when you tell your parents what your teacher said.

rv.summary: Direct speech gives exact words in quotation marks; reported speech gives the meaning, often with 'that'. After a past reporting verb, tenses move back and pronouns, time and place words change.

Shift tenses back after said/asked/told.
Change pronouns and time/place words.
remember: am/is → was, are → were, will → would, can → could, simple past → past perfect.

Questions: asked + if/whether or the wh-word, in statement order. Commands: told/ordered + to.
traps: Don't keep question word order: 'where he was going', not 'where was he going'.
Don't use 'that' for a yes/no question; use 'if' or 'whether'.
Don't forget to change the pronoun and the tense: 'Ria said that she was hungry.'

topics.t: Humorous poems: rhyme, rhythm and exaggeration
topics.h: Can a paratha be used as a brick? In a funny poem, anything can happen!
p: 'A Concrete Example' is a humorous poem that has fun with words and their meanings.
Rhyme: words that end with the same sound, like thick and brick. A rhyme scheme labels line endings with letters: AABB means lines 1-2 rhyme and lines 3-4 rhyme; ABAB means lines 1-3 and 2-4 rhyme.
Rhythm is the beat of a poem, made by the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables. A bouncy rhythm makes a funny poem fun to read aloud.
Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration for effect: 'I've told you a million times!'
Onomatopoeia is a word that imitates a sound (crack, buzz, splash). Alliteration repeats the same first consonant sound in nearby words (Bunty bought big balloons).

ex.q: Read this original poem: 'Our cook made parathas so heavy and thick, / Our dog used one as a brand-new brick. / Papa took a bite and his jaw went CRACK! / Now he wants his teeth and his money back!' Think it through: what is the rhyme scheme, and where is the exaggeration?
st: Line endings: thick (A), brick (A), crack (B), back (B).
So the rhyme scheme is AABB.
No real paratha could be used as a brick: that is hyperbole.
'CRACK' imitates a sound, so it is onomatopoeia that adds to the fun.
ex.a: The rhyme scheme is AABB, and the paratha-as-a-brick line is hyperbole.

topics.rl: Advertising jingles, cricket chants and birthday rhymes use rhyme, rhythm and exaggeration to stick in your memory.

rv.summary: 'A Concrete Example' is a humorous poem that has fun with words. We learn rhyme, rhyme scheme, rhythm, hyperbole, onomatopoeia and alliteration.
focus: Find rhyming words by their ending sound.
Work out AABB and ABAB rhyme schemes.
Spot hyperbole, onomatopoeia and alliteration.

Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration for effect.
Onomatopoeia imitates a sound (crack, buzz, splash); alliteration repeats the same first consonant sound in nearby words.
traps: Rhyme is about the ending sound, not the spelling or first letter: 'laugh' rhymes with 'half'.
Don't read ABAB as pairs of neighbouring lines.
Alliteration is not rhyme at the end of lines.

topics.t: Fun with language: puns, homophones and homonyms
topics.h: Why did the student carry a ladder to class? She wanted to go to high school! Words with two meanings make the best jokes.
p: A pun is a joke that plays on a word with two meanings, or on two words that sound alike.
The title 'A Concrete Example' can be read two ways: 'concrete' means real and specific, and it is also the building material made of cement, sand, gravel and water.
Homophones sound the same but have different spellings and meanings: flour/flower, pair/pear, knight/night, peace/piece, weather/whether, stationary/stationery.
Homonyms have the same spelling and sound but different meanings: bat (cricket bat / flying animal), bank (money bank / river bank), bark (a dog's bark / a tree's bark).
Literal meaning is the plain meaning of the words; figurative meaning is a special or imaginative meaning. 'A piece of cake' literally is cake, but figuratively means 'very easy'.

ex.q: Think it through: 'Why did the student carry a ladder to class? She wanted to go to high school!' Explain the pun.
st: Find the word or phrase with two meanings: 'high school'.
Meaning 1: a level of school for older students.
Meaning 2: a school that is high up, so you would need a ladder.
The joke works because both meanings fit at once.
ex.a: 'High school' means a senior school and also, jokingly, a school that is high up, which is why she needs a ladder.

topics.rl: Newspaper headlines, shop names and greeting cards love puns, like a tailor's shop called 'Sew Good' (it sounds like 'so good'). Spotting them makes reading more fun.

rv.summary: A pun plays on a word with two meanings or on words that sound alike, like the title 'A Concrete Example'. We also learn homophones, homonyms, and literal versus figurative meaning.
focus: Explain how a pun works using both meanings.
Tell homophones from homonyms.
Use context to pick the right meaning or spelling.
remember: Homophones sound the same but have different spellings and meanings: flour/flower, pair/pear, knight/night, stationary/stationery.

traps: A homophone is spelt differently; same spelling and sound with two meanings is a homonym.
Don't mix up 'stationary' (not moving) and 'stationery' (paper, pens).
Don't take a figurative phrase literally: 'a piece of cake' means very easy.

topics.t: Folk wisdom tales, morals and proverbs
topics.h: Two brothers, one big basket of mangoes and a fight that could last forever. Can one wise sentence fix it?
p: The lesson 'Wisdom Paves the Way' is a folk story in which clear, wise thinking opens a way out of a difficult problem.

Folk tales are stories passed down by word of mouth over many generations, so their first authors are usually unknown. India has a rich storytelling tradition, including folk tales and well-loved fable collections like the Panchatantra.
Folk tales often have a simple setting, a problem, a wise or clever character, and a moral, which is the lesson the story teaches.
A proverb is a short, well-known saying that gives advice: 'Look before you leap', 'A stitch in time saves nine', 'Two heads are better than one'.
'Wisdom' is a noun. Its adjective is 'wise' and its adverb is 'wisely'.

ex.q: Read this original tale: Two brothers in a Rajasthan village quarrelled over a basket of mangoes left by their grandfather. Each said the other would cheat. Old Gomti-ma listened and said, "Let one of you divide the mangoes into two heaps, and let the other choose first." The quarrel ended at once. Think it through: why does her plan make the sharing fair?
st: One brother divides; the other picks first.
If the divider makes one heap smaller, the other brother will take the bigger heap.
So the divider is forced to make the two heaps as equal as he can.
Neither brother can complain: one made the heaps, the other chose.
ex.a: The divider must make equal heaps, because any bigger heap would be chosen by the other brother.

topics.rl: When two friends share a samosa, one cuts and the other chooses. You are using Gomti-ma's wisdom!

rv.summary: 'Wisdom Paves the Way' is a folk story in which clear, wise thinking opens a way out of a difficult problem. Folk tales are passed down by word of mouth and teach a moral; proverbs give short advice.
focus: Explain why a wise solution works, like 'one divides, the other chooses'.
Know the features of a folk tale and what a moral is.
Match a proverb to a situation.
remember: A proverb is a short, well-known saying that gives advice: 'Look before you leap', 'A stitch in time saves nine', 'Two heads are better than one'.
The moral is the lesson the story teaches.
wisdom (noun), wise (adjective), wisely (adverb).
traps: Don't mix up the moral (lesson) with the setting (time and place).
Don't confuse the adjective 'wise' with the adverb 'wisely'.
Don't pick a familiar proverb without matching its meaning.

topics.t: Problem solving: steps and linking words
topics.h: A wise person does not panic. She goes step by step. And when we explain steps, little linking words do a big job!
p: Problem solving has clear steps: understand the problem, think of possible solutions, choose the best one, try it out, and check whether it worked.
Sequence connectors show the order of steps: first, next, then, after that, finally.
Cause and effect connectors join a reason and a result: because, as, so, therefore, as a result. 'Because' introduces the reason; 'so' introduces the result.
Contrast connectors show a difference or surprise: but, however, although, though.

ex.q: Think it through: The plants in Class 8's garden dry up every summer holiday. Explain how to solve this using connectors.
st: First, understand the problem: no one waters the plants during the holidays.
Next, list solutions: a watering rota, a drip bottle, or moving pots to shade.
Then, choose the best one: a rota of students who live nearby, because it is simple and free.
Finally, check after the holidays whether the plants survived.
ex.a: First understand, next list ideas, then choose and try the best one, and finally check the result.

topics.rl: Recipes, science experiments and instructions for a board game all use sequence words like first, then and finally.

rv.summary: Problem solving has clear steps: understand the problem, think of solutions, choose the best, try it and check. Connectors show sequence, cause and effect, and contrast.
focus: Order the steps of solving a problem.
Use sequence connectors: first, next, then, after that, finally.
Choose cause-effect and contrast connectors correctly.
remember: Cause and effect: because, as, so, therefore, as a result. 'Because' introduces the reason; 'so' introduces the result.
Contrast: but, however, although, though.
Sequence: first, next, then, after that, finally.
traps: Don't mix up 'because' (reason) with 'so' (result).
'Although' shows contrast, not a reason.
Don't rush to a solution before understanding the problem.

topics.t: Phrasal verbs for solving problems
topics.h: 'Give up', 'give in', 'give away': change one little word and the meaning flips! Meet phrasal verbs.
p: A phrasal verb is a verb followed by a particle (a small word such as up, out, into, on, off) that together have a new meaning.

Problem-solving phrasal verbs: figure out (understand or solve), work out (find the answer), come up with (think of an idea), look into (investigate), sort out (fix), carry on (continue), give up (stop trying).
Changing the particle changes the meaning: give up (stop trying), give in (accept defeat), give away (hand out for free).
More useful ones: put off (postpone), look after (take care of), run out of (have none left), find out (discover), turn down (refuse).

ex.q: Think it through: Replace the words in brackets with a phrasal verb. 'Tara (thought of) a clever plan to save water in the school.'
st: The meaning is 'produced an idea'.
The phrasal verb for producing an idea is 'come up with'.
The sentence is in the past, so use 'came up with'.
ex.a: Tara came up with a clever plan to save water in the school.

topics.rl: Everyday English is full of phrasal verbs: 'Switch off the fan', 'Pick up your bag', 'We ran out of sugar'.

rv.summary: A phrasal verb is a verb plus a particle such as up, out, into, on or off, which together have a new meaning. Changing the particle changes the meaning.
focus: Know problem-solving phrasal verbs and their meanings.
Notice how the particle changes the meaning: give up, give in, give away.
Replace a word with the right phrasal verb in the correct tense.
remember: figure out (understand or solve), work out (find the answer), come up with (think of an idea), look into (investigate), sort out (fix), carry on (continue), give up (stop trying).
give up (stop trying), give in (accept defeat), give away (hand out for free).
put off (postpone), look after (take care of), run out of (have none left), find out (discover), turn down (refuse).

'Put off' means postponed, not cancelled for good.

topics.ch: A Tale of Valour: Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
topics.t: Major Somnath Sharma: the first Param Vir Chakra
topics.h: India's highest award for bravery has a very special first name on its list. Whose is it, and what did he do?
p: The lesson is a true account of courage: how Major Somnath Sharma led his soldiers in the Battle of Badgam.
The Param Vir Chakra (PVC) is India's highest military award for gallantry, given for the greatest bravery in the face of the enemy.
Major Somnath Sharma of the 4th Battalion of the Kumaon Regiment was the first-ever recipient of the Param Vir Chakra.

The Battle of Badgam was fought on 3 November 1947, near Srinagar in Jammu and Kashmir. His company held its position against a much larger attacking force until more troops arrived, helping to protect the Srinagar airfield.
He gave his life in this battle, so he received the award posthumously, which means after his death.

ex.q: Read this original tribute: 'His arm was in a plaster cast, yet he would not stay behind. At Badgam he moved from post to post, cheering his men and guiding them, and he did not leave his position.' Think it through: what does this tell us about his character?
st: Notice the injury: his arm was in a plaster cast.
Notice what he did anyway: he went with his men and moved from post to post.
Notice how he treated his soldiers: he cheered and guided them.
Put it together: he was brave, dutiful and a caring leader.
ex.a: He was courageous and devoted to duty, and he led and encouraged his men even when he was injured.

topics.rl: The National War Memorial in New Delhi honours India's brave soldiers, including Param Vir Chakra recipients like Major Somnath Sharma.

rv.summary: Major Somnath Sharma of the Kumaon Regiment led his soldiers in the Battle of Badgam on 3 November 1947 near Srinagar and became the first-ever recipient of the Param Vir Chakra. He received it posthumously.
focus: Recall key facts: PVC, Kumaon Regiment, Battle of Badgam, 3 November 1947.
Explain what his actions show about his character.
Know the meanings of 'posthumously' and 'valour'.
remember: The Param Vir Chakra (PVC) is India's highest military award for gallantry.
Battle of Badgam: 3 November 1947, near Srinagar in Jammu and Kashmir.
Posthumously means after his death.
traps: Don't mix up the battle date with Independence Day or Republic Day.
'Posthumously' has nothing to do with the postal service.
Valour (great courage) is not 'value'.

topics.t: Courage: vocabulary and abstract nouns
topics.h: You cannot hold courage in your hand, put it in your bag or weigh it. So what kind of noun is it?
p: Words close in meaning to courage: bravery, valour, gallantry, heroism, fearlessness. Opposites: cowardice, timidity, fearfulness.
An abstract noun names a quality, feeling or idea that we cannot see or touch: courage, honesty, freedom, kindness, loyalty.
Many abstract nouns come from adjectives: brave → bravery, loyal → loyalty, strong → strength, proud → pride, wise → wisdom, free → freedom, kind → kindness.
Some come from common nouns or verbs: hero → heroism, friend → friendship and decide → decision.
Courage is not only for soldiers. Telling the truth, standing up for someone who is being teased, or trying again after failing also takes courage.

ex.q: Think it through: Find the abstract nouns in this sentence: 'The soldier's bravery and loyalty earned the respect of the whole nation.'
st: Check each noun: soldier, bravery, loyalty, respect, nation.
A soldier and a nation can be seen, so they are not abstract.
Bravery, loyalty and respect are qualities or feelings that cannot be touched.
ex.a: bravery, loyalty, respect

topics.rl: The Pradhan Mantri Rashtriya Bal Puraskar honours children for achievements that include bravery, such as saving someone in danger.

rv.summary: Courage has synonyms like bravery, valour and gallantry, and opposites like cowardice. Abstract nouns name qualities or ideas we cannot see or touch, and many are formed from adjectives, nouns or verbs.

Identify abstract nouns in a sentence.
Form abstract nouns correctly.

hero → heroism, friend → friendship, decide → decision.
traps: Don't add -ness or -ly by habit: the noun of 'strong' is 'strength'.
Don't use an adjective where a noun is needed: 'praised for his bravery'.
Courage does not only mean fighting; telling the truth can take courage.

topics.t: Telling a true story: past tenses
topics.h: A true story already happened. To tell it clearly, you need the right past tense at the right moment.
p: Simple past tells a completed action at a definite time: The battle began at dawn. We watched the parade yesterday.
Past continuous (was/were + verb-ing) shows an action in progress in the past: The soldiers were guarding the airfield.
Past continuous + simple past shows a longer action interrupted by a shorter one: We were eating dinner when the lights went off.
Past perfect (had + past participle) shows an action completed before another past action: The film had started when we reached the hall.
Learn irregular verbs: fight-fought-fought, hold-held-held, lead-led-led, give-gave-given, win-won-won, write-wrote-written.

ex.q: Think it through: Join these two sentences using the past perfect. 'The match finished. Then we reached the stadium.'
st: Find the earlier action: the match finished.
The earlier action takes the past perfect: had finished.
The later action stays in simple past: reached.
Join them with 'when'.
ex.a: The match had finished when we reached the stadium.

topics.rl: Diaries, news reports and history books use past tenses to tell what happened, what was happening, and what had already happened.

rv.summary: To tell a true story we use simple past, past continuous and past perfect. Past continuous shows an action in progress, often interrupted by a simple past action; past perfect shows the earlier of two past actions.
focus: Choose the right past tense from the meaning.
Join two past actions with past perfect for the earlier one.
Learn irregular verb forms.
remember: Past continuous: was/were + verb-ing. Past perfect: had + past participle.
'We were eating dinner when the lights went off.'
fight-fought-fought, hold-held-held, lead-led-led, give-gave-given, win-won-won, write-wrote-written.
traps: Don't add -ed to an irregular verb: 'led', not 'leaded'.
Don't use simple past for the longer, interrupted action: 'While I was doing my homework'.
