topics.t: A poem on kindness: reading and figurative language
topics.h: One small act on a crowded bus can warm a whole crowd. Poems know how to show that.
p: 'Somebody's Mother' is a poem about kindness to an elderly person. Its theme: every elder is somebody's dear one, so treat them as you would treat your own family.
The theme is the main idea of a poem. The speaker is the voice telling the poem. A stanza is a group of lines in a poem.
A simile compares two things using 'like' or 'as': warm as sunshine. A metaphor compares without 'like' or 'as': his smile was a lamp.
Personification gives human qualities to non-human things: The old bus groaned up the hill.
Empathy means imagining how another person feels. Kind actions often begin with empathy.

ex.q: Read this original poem: 'The bus was full, the seats were gone, / An old man held the rail alone; / A schoolgirl stood and gave her place, / A thank-you bloomed upon his face. / "He's someone's grandpa, just like mine," / She thought, and the bus felt warm as sunshine.' Think it through: find one metaphor and one simile.
st: A metaphor compares without 'like' or 'as'.
'A thank-you bloomed upon his face' compares his grateful smile to a flower opening: metaphor.
A simile uses 'like' or 'as'.
'warm as sunshine' compares the bus's feeling to sunshine using 'as': simile.
ex.a: Metaphor: 'A thank-you bloomed upon his face'. Simile: 'warm as sunshine'.

topics.rl: Giving your seat to an elder in a bus or metro, or helping a neighbour carry vegetables, is the kindness this poem celebrates.

rv.summary: 'Somebody's Mother' is a poem about kindness to an elderly person: every elder is somebody's dear one, so treat them like your own family. We also learn theme, speaker, stanza, simile, metaphor, personification and empathy.
focus: State the theme of the poem.
Tell a simile from a metaphor and spot personification.
Explain how empathy leads to kind actions.
remember: The theme is the main idea of a poem; a stanza is a group of lines in a poem.
A simile compares using 'like' or 'as'; a metaphor compares without 'like' or 'as'.
Personification gives human qualities to non-human things.
Empathy means imagining how another person feels.
traps: Don't call every comparison a simile; without 'like' or 'as' it is a metaphor.
Don't confuse personification with simile: 'The old bus groaned' is personification.
A group of lines in a poem is a stanza, not a paragraph.

topics.t: Respect for elders: polite language and modals
topics.h: 'Give me water!' or 'Could you please pass me some water?' Same request, very different respect!
p: Modals are helping verbs that show ability, permission, advice, offers and more: can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must.
Polite requests: Could you...? Would you...? 'Could you please help me?' sounds more polite than 'Can you help me?'
Asking permission: May I...? (formal, very polite) or Can I...? (informal). 'May I come in, ma'am?'
Offering help: Shall I...? Would you like...? 'Shall I carry your bag, Dadi?' Giving advice: should. 'You should rest, Nanaji.'
Respect also shows in words like please, thank you and sorry, in a gentle tone, and in listening patiently when elders speak.

ex.q: Think it through: Make this more polite and respectful: 'Uncle, move your bag. I want to sit.'
st: Start with a polite modal for a request: Could you...
Add 'please'.
Explain the need gently instead of demanding.
Thank the person.
ex.a: Uncle, could you please move your bag a little so that I can sit? Thank you!

topics.rl: At a family wedding or a visit to Nani's house, polite phrases like 'May I help?' and 'Shall I bring you tea?' make elders feel cared for.

rv.summary: We show respect for elders through polite language and modals. Use could/would for polite requests, may for formal permission, shall for offers and should for advice.
focus: Make requests polite with Could you...? / Would you...?
Choose the right modal for permission, offer, advice, ability or a rule.
Recognise respectful and rude tone.
remember: Polite requests: 'Could you please help me?' sounds more polite than 'Can you help me?'
May I...? (formal, very polite); Can I...? (informal).
Offering help: Shall I...? Would you like...? Advice: should.
'Could' is the past of 'can' for ability; 'must not' means it is not allowed.
traps: Don't confuse permission (may) with obligation (must).
'Shall I...?' here offers help; it does not just show the future.
Don't use present 'can' for a past ability; use 'could'.

topics.ch: Verghese Kurien — I Too Had A Dream
topics.t: Verghese Kurien and the White Revolution
topics.h: India once did not have enough milk for its children. Today it produces more milk than any other country. Who dreamed this big?
p: The lesson tells the story of Dr Verghese Kurien, whose dream was to make dairy farmers prosper. 'I Too Had a Dream' is also the title of his memoir.
Verghese Kurien was born on 26 November 1921 in Kozhikode (Calicut), Kerala. In 1949 he was posted to Anand in Gujarat, where he chose to stay and work with dairy farmers.
He is called the 'Father of the White Revolution'. The White Revolution was the huge rise in India's milk production.
Operation Flood, launched in 1970 by the National Dairy Development Board (NDDB) under his leadership, linked village milk producers to cities across India. Kurien was the first chairman of the NDDB.
Today India is the world's largest producer of milk, and his birthday, 26 November, is celebrated as National Milk Day.

ex.q: Read this original passage: 'Kurien was an engineer, not a farmer. Yet when he saw how farmers in Anand got very little money for their milk, he decided to stay and help them. He believed that if farmers owned their own dairy, they would get a fair price.' Think it through: what was Kurien's dream?
st: Notice the problem: farmers got very little money for their milk.
Notice his decision: he stayed in Anand to help them.
Notice his belief: farmers should own their dairy to get a fair price.
So his dream was about fairness and farmers' prosperity.
ex.a: His dream was that dairy farmers would own and run their own dairies and get a fair price for their milk.

topics.rl: The packet of milk or curd that reaches your home every morning is part of a supply chain that grew out of the White Revolution.

rv.summary: Dr Verghese Kurien, the 'Father of the White Revolution', dreamt of making dairy farmers prosper and led Operation Flood, launched in 1970 by the NDDB. His birthday, 26 November, is National Milk Day.
focus: Recall key facts: born 26 November 1921 in Kozhikode, Kerala; posted to Anand, Gujarat in 1949.
Know Operation Flood (1970, NDDB) and his memoir 'I Too Had a Dream'.
Explain what his dream was.
remember: The White Revolution was the huge rise in India's milk production.
Operation Flood: launched in 1970 by the NDDB; Kurien was the first chairman of the NDDB.
National Milk Day: 26 November, Kurien's birthday.
traps: Don't mix up the White Revolution (milk) with the Green Revolution (grains).
Don't confuse National Milk Day (26 November) with World Milk Day (1 June).
Kurien was born in Kerala, not in Gujarat where he worked.

topics.ch: Verghese Kurien — I Too Had A Dream
topics.t: Amul and the cooperative way
topics.h: What happens when thousands of farmers who each own just one or two buffaloes join hands? They build one of India's biggest dairies!
p: A cooperative is a group owned and run by its members for their shared benefit. Each member has a say (one member, one vote) and profits are shared among members.
In 1946, dairy farmers of Kaira (Kheda) district formed the Kaira District Cooperative Milk Producers' Union at Anand, Gujarat, led by Tribhuvandas Patel. Its products later took the brand name Amul.
Amul is often explained as 'Anand Milk Union Limited'. Kurien worked with this union and helped it grow.
The 'Anand pattern' has three levels: village dairy cooperative societies collect milk, a district union processes it, and a state federation markets it.
Because the farmers own the system, middlemen are removed and farmers receive a fairer price for their milk.

ex.q: Read this original passage: 'Every morning and evening, Lakshmiben carries her buffalo's milk to the village society. The milk is tested for fat, and she is paid according to its quality. At the end of the year, she also gets a share of the profit, because she is a member.' Think it through: why is this a cooperative?
st: Lakshmiben is a member, not just a seller.
She is paid fairly, by the quality of her milk.
Profits are shared with members like her.
Ownership and benefit belong to the members: that is a cooperative.
ex.a: It is a cooperative because the farmers are members who own it, are paid fairly and share its profits.

topics.rl: Housing societies in cities, many sugar mills in Maharashtra, and cooperative banks in towns are also cooperatives run by their members.

rv.summary: A cooperative is owned and run by its members for their shared benefit. In 1946 Kaira dairy farmers, led by Tribhuvandas Patel, formed a union at Anand whose products became Amul, and the Anand pattern removes middlemen.
focus: Define a cooperative: one member, one vote, shared profits.
Know the three levels of the Anand pattern.
Explain how cooperatives give farmers a fairer price.
remember: A cooperative is a group owned and run by its members for their shared benefit.
Anand pattern: village societies collect milk, a district union processes it, a state federation markets it.
Amul is often explained as 'Anand Milk Union Limited'.
The prefix 'co-' means together.
traps: Not every business or group working together is a cooperative; members must own it.
Don't mix up the three levels: the village society collects milk from farmers.
Don't confuse 'co-' (together) with 'counter-' (against).

topics.ch: Verghese Kurien — I Too Had A Dream
topics.t: Describing a process: active and passive voice
topics.h: 'The farmer milks the buffalo' or 'The buffalo is milked'? Both are correct. The choice depends on what you want to highlight.
p: In the active voice, the subject does the action: The society collects the milk.
In the passive voice, the receiver of the action becomes the subject: The milk is collected by the society.
Passive = a form of 'be' + past participle. Present: is/are collected. Past: was/were collected. Future: will be collected. Present continuous: is being collected. With modals: can be collected.
The doer is shown with 'by' (by the society), or left out when it is unknown or unimportant: The milk is pasteurised and packed.
The passive is common when describing processes, because the steps matter more than who does them.

ex.q: Think it through: Change to the passive voice: 'The workers packed the milk in pouches.'
st: Object of the active sentence: the milk. It becomes the subject.
The verb 'packed' is simple past, so use was/were + past participle: was packed.
Add the doer with 'by': by the workers.
Keep the rest: in pouches.
ex.a: The milk was packed in pouches by the workers.

topics.rl: Instructions and science textbooks often use the passive: 'The solution is heated', 'The seeds are sown in June'.

rv.summary: In the active voice the subject does the action; in the passive the receiver becomes the subject. The passive (be + past participle) is common in describing processes because the steps matter more than who does them.
focus: Change active to passive and back without changing the tense.
Use the right passive form for each tense.
Know when to leave out the doer.
remember: Passive = a form of 'be' + past participle.
is/are collected; was/were collected; will be collected; is being collected; can be collected.
The doer is shown with 'by', or left out when unknown or unimportant.
traps: Don't change the tense while changing the voice.
Don't use the past tense instead of the past participle: 'was written', not 'was wrote'.
Don't forget 'being' in the present continuous passive: 'is being pasteurised'.

topics.ch: The Case of the Fifth Word
topics.t: Mystery stories: clues, suspects and red herrings
topics.h: The last gulab jamun has vanished from the fridge. Three suspects, one sticky clue. Ready, detective?
p: 'The Case of the Fifth Word' is a mystery story in which a puzzle is solved by careful observation and logical thinking.
A mystery story usually has: a puzzle or crime, a detective, suspects, clues, at least one false lead, and a final reveal where the solution is explained.

Key words: clue (a sign that helps solve a puzzle), suspect (a person who may be guilty), culprit (the person who actually did it), alibi (proof that a suspect was somewhere else), motive (the reason for doing it), witness (someone who saw something), evidence (facts or objects that show what happened).
A red herring is a misleading clue that points the reader the wrong way.
A good detective separates facts from guesses and checks every clue.

ex.q: Read this original mystery: 'The last gulab jamun vanished from the Iyer family's fridge. Grandma said, "I was at the market all evening," and the shopkeeper agreed. Kavya pointed at the cat, but the fridge door was too heavy for a cat to open. Detective Divya then spotted sweet syrup on her brother Ravi's homework book.' Think it through: who is the likely culprit, and what is the red herring?
st: Grandma has an alibi: the shopkeeper confirms she was at the market.
The cat is suggested, but it could not open the heavy fridge door: that is the red herring.
The syrup on Ravi's book is evidence that links him to the sweet.
So Ravi is the likely culprit.
ex.a: Ravi is the likely culprit. The cat is the red herring.

topics.rl: Detective stories like the Feluda tales by Satyajit Ray and the Byomkesh Bakshi stories are loved across India because readers try to solve the case before the detective does.

rv.summary: 'The Case of the Fifth Word' is a mystery solved by careful observation and logical thinking. Mystery stories have a puzzle, a detective, suspects, clues, a false lead and a final reveal.
focus: Know mystery words: clue, suspect, culprit, alibi, motive, witness, evidence.
Spot a red herring and identify the likely culprit from clues.
Separate facts from guesses.
remember: Alibi: proof that a suspect was somewhere else. Motive: the reason for doing it.
Suspect: a person who may be guilty. Culprit: the person who actually did it.
A red herring is a misleading clue that points the reader the wrong way.
traps: Don't confuse alibi with motive.
A suspect is not the same as the culprit.
Guesses and opinions are not evidence.

topics.ch: The Case of the Fifth Word
topics.t: Logical deduction and inference
topics.h: A secret message is hidden in plain sight. Only a careful reader will find it!
p: An inference is a conclusion you reach from clues in the text plus what you already know. 'Her umbrella dripped on the floor' lets you infer that it was raining.
A deduction follows strictly from facts: if 'All of Class 8B went on the trip' and 'Neha is in 8B' are true, then 'Neha went on the trip' must be true.
Separate a fact (can be checked), an inference (a sensible conclusion from clues) and a guess (no clue supports it).
Read closely: one small word like 'not', 'only', 'all' or 'some' can change the whole meaning.
Codes and hidden messages use patterns, such as the first letter of each line (an acrostic) or one chosen word from each sentence.

ex.q: Think it through: Find the hidden place in this note by reading the first letter of each line: 'Look under the mat / In the blue box / Behind the clock / Raju hid it / And then ran / Right back home / Yes, go now!'
st: Take the first letter of each line: L, I, B, R, A, R, Y.
Join them: LIBRARY.
Check that the word makes sense as a hiding place: it does.
ex.a: LIBRARY

topics.rl: Doctors infer illnesses from symptoms, and you infer that a friend is upset from their face and silence.

rv.summary: An inference is a conclusion from clues plus what you already know, while a deduction follows strictly from facts. Read closely, because small words like 'not', 'only', 'all' and 'some' change the meaning.
focus: Tell a fact, an inference and a guess apart.
Make deductions from 'all', 'some' and 'only' statements.
Find hidden words in codes like acrostics.
remember: An inference is a conclusion you reach from clues in the text plus what you already know.
Fact (can be checked), inference (a sensible conclusion from clues), guess (no clue supports it).
An acrostic uses the first letter of each line.
traps: 'Some' does not mean 'all'.
Don't ignore the word 'only'.
Don't add ideas the facts do not support; use all the clues, not just one.

topics.ch: The Case of the Fifth Word
topics.t: Modals of deduction: must, might and can't
topics.h: A detective never says 'I think maybe perhaps...'. She says 'It MUST be him!' or 'It CAN'T be her!' Modals show how sure we are.
p: Modals of deduction show how certain we are about something.
must = almost certain it is true: The ground is wet. It must have rained.
might / may / could = possible, but not sure: He might be at the library.
can't = almost certain it is NOT true: She can't be at home; I just saw her at school.
For the past, use modal + have + past participle: must have taken, might have forgotten, can't have seen.

ex.q: Think it through: The cake tin is empty. There are crumbs on Tinku's shirt. His sister was away all day. Complete: 'Tinku ___ eaten the cake. His sister ___ eaten it.'
st: The crumbs on Tinku's shirt make it almost certain: must have.
His sister was away all day, so it is almost impossible: can't have.
Use have + past participle (eaten) for past deductions.
ex.a: Tinku must have eaten the cake. His sister can't have eaten it.

topics.rl: We use these every day: 'You must be hungry after the match', 'Mummy might be stuck in traffic', 'That can't be the bus, it's too early'.

rv.summary: Modals of deduction show how certain we are: must (almost certain), might/may/could (possible), can't (almost certainly not). For the past, use modal + have + past participle.
focus: Choose must, might/may/could or can't from the clues.
Form past deductions correctly.
Tell deduction 'must' from duty 'must'.
remember: must = almost certain it is true; might / may / could = possible; can't = almost certain it is NOT true.
Past: must have taken, might have forgotten, can't have seen.
traps: Don't use 'has' or 'had' after a modal: 'must have forgotten'.
'Might' does not show strong certainty.
'Must' has two uses: duty and deduction.

topics.t: Fantasy tales and the shape of a story
topics.h: What would you paint if everything you painted came alive? A fantasy tale lets you imagine exactly that.
p: 'The Magic Brush of Dreams' is a fantasy tale about art, imagination and using a gift fairly.
Fantasy stories include things that cannot happen in real life: magic objects, magical powers, talking animals or imaginary worlds. Yet they often carry real lessons about good and bad choices.
Every story has a setting (where and when), characters (who), and a plot (what happens).
A plot usually moves through: exposition (introduction), conflict (the problem), rising action (things get harder), climax (the turning point), and resolution (how it ends).
The protagonist is the main character. The antagonist is the person or force that works against the protagonist.

ex.q: Read this original tale: 'In a dry village of Bundelkhand, a boy named Kabir found an old paint pot. Whatever he painted for others came alive, but nothing he painted for himself ever moved. When the village well dried up, Kabir painted dark rain clouds across the sky, and rain poured down. A greedy trader demanded a painted mountain of gold, but Kabir refused and painted a garden for the children instead.' Think it through: name the conflict and one fantasy element.
st: The problem in the village is that the well has dried up; a second conflict is the greedy trader's demand.
A fantasy element is something impossible in real life: paintings that come alive.
The resolution: Kabir uses his gift for others, not for greed.
ex.a: Conflict: the dried-up well (and the greedy trader). Fantasy element: paintings that come to life.

topics.rl: Animated films, comics and many grandparents' bedtime stories use fantasy to make us think about real values like honesty and sharing.

rv.summary: 'The Magic Brush of Dreams' is a fantasy tale about art, imagination and using a gift fairly. Every story has a setting, characters and a plot that moves from exposition to resolution.
focus: Identify fantasy elements and the lesson they carry.
Name the parts of a plot in order.
Identify the protagonist, antagonist, setting and conflict.
remember: Plot: exposition (introduction), conflict (the problem), rising action, climax (the turning point), resolution (how it ends).
The protagonist is the main character; the antagonist works against the protagonist.
Setting (where and when), characters (who), plot (what happens).
traps: Don't confuse the climax with the resolution (ending).
Don't confuse protagonist with antagonist.
Not every interesting event is fantasy; it must be impossible in real life.

topics.t: Art and justice: values, word families and Indian art
topics.h: A brush can make a picture. Can it also make things fair? Let's explore the words of justice.
p: Justice means fairness: giving people what they rightly deserve. In stories, justice is done when the honest are helped and the greedy are stopped.
Word family: just (adjective) → justice (noun) → justly (adverb); unjust and injustice are the opposites.

Negative prefixes: un- (unfair, unkind), dis- (dishonest, disagree), in- (inactive, incorrect, injustice). im- is used before p, m or b (impossible, immature, imbalance), il- before l (illegal), ir- before r (irregular, irresponsible).
Indian folk and traditional art: Madhubani (Bihar), Warli (Maharashtra), Pattachitra (Odisha), Gond (Madhya Pradesh), Tanjore painting (Tamil Nadu), Phad (Rajasthan).
Art can speak for justice: artists paint, sing and write to show unfairness and to imagine a better world.

ex.q: Think it through: Add the correct prefix to make the opposite of each word: legal, possible, responsible, honest.
st: 'legal' starts with l, so use il-: illegal.
'possible' starts with p, so use im-: impossible.
'responsible' starts with r, so use ir-: irresponsible.
'honest' takes dis-: dishonest.
ex.a: illegal, impossible, irresponsible, dishonest

topics.rl: Warli wall paintings show village life with simple shapes, and Madhubani art is painted on walls, paper and cloth. Both can be seen at state handicraft melas.

rv.summary: Justice means fairness: giving people what they rightly deserve. We learn the 'just' word family, negative prefixes and traditional Indian art forms and their states.
focus: Know just → justice → justly, and unjust / injustice.
Choose the right negative prefix.
Match Indian art forms with their states.
remember: just (adjective) → justice (noun) → justly (adverb); opposites: unjust, injustice.
im- before p, m or b; il- before l; ir- before r; also un-, dis-, in-.
Madhubani (Bihar), Warli (Maharashtra), Pattachitra (Odisha), Gond (Madhya Pradesh), Tanjore (Tamil Nadu), Phad (Rajasthan).
traps: Don't use un- for every opposite: illegal, irresponsible, dishonest.
The opposite of the noun 'justice' is 'injustice', not 'unjustice'.
Don't mix up Warli (Maharashtra) with Pattachitra (Odisha).

topics.t: Describing art: degrees of comparison
topics.h: Kabir's first painting was bright, his second was brighter, and his last was the brightest of all. Comparing is a painter's best tool!
p: Adjectives have three degrees: positive (bright), comparative (brighter, for two), superlative (brightest, for three or more). Use 'than' after a comparative and 'the' before a superlative.
Short adjectives add -er/-est: tall, taller, tallest. Double the last consonant after a single short vowel: big, bigger, biggest. Change -y to -i: pretty, prettier, prettiest.
Long adjectives use more/most: colourful, more colourful, most colourful.
Irregular forms: good-better-best, bad-worse-worst, many/much-more-most, little-less-least.
Equality uses as...as: 'This Warli painting is as detailed as that one.' Not as/so...as shows a difference.

ex.q: Think it through: Fill in the blanks: 'Of all the paintings in the mela, Kabir's was the ___ (good). It was ___ (colourful) than the trader's poster.'
st: 'Of all' compares more than two, so use the superlative of good: best.
'than' compares two things, so use the comparative.
'Colourful' is long, so use 'more': more colourful.
ex.a: the best; more colourful

topics.rl: Art competitions, cricket commentary and shopping all need comparisons: the best painting, a faster bowler, a cheaper kurta.

rv.summary: Adjectives have three degrees: positive, comparative (for two, with 'than') and superlative (for three or more, with 'the'). Short adjectives add -er/-est, long ones use more/most, and some are irregular.
focus: Choose comparative or superlative from the sentence.
Apply spelling rules: doubling and -y to -i.
Use irregular forms and as...as.
remember: Short: tall, taller, tallest; big, bigger, biggest; pretty, prettier, prettiest.
Long: colourful, more colourful, most colourful.
Irregular: good-better-best, bad-worse-worst, many/much-more-most, little-less-least.
Equality uses as...as; not as/so...as shows a difference.
traps: Don't use 'more' and '-er' together: 'brighter', not 'more brighter'.
Don't add -est to a long adjective: 'the most beautiful'.
Don't confuse 'worse' (comparative) with 'worst' (superlative).

topics.t: Natural wonders of India
topics.h: Bridges that grow, a lake with floating islands and a desert of white salt. These are not fairy tales; they are in India!
p: The lesson 'Spectacular Wonders' takes readers on a journey through amazing natural places and shows how to describe them vividly.
Living root bridges of Meghalaya are grown, not built: Khasi and Jaintia communities guide the roots of rubber fig trees across streams until they form strong bridges.
Loktak Lake in Manipur has floating masses of plants and soil called phumdis. On it lies Keibul Lamjao, the only floating national park in the world and the home of the sangai deer.
Lonar Lake in Maharashtra lies in a crater formed when a meteorite struck the Earth. The Great Rann of Kutch in Gujarat is a vast white salt desert.

The Valley of Flowers in Uttarakhand blooms with wildflowers in the monsoon months; the Sundarbans in West Bengal is a mangrove forest, home to the Royal Bengal tiger; the Marble Rocks at Bhedaghat in Madhya Pradesh line the Narmada river.

ex.q: Read this original passage: 'At Bhedaghat, the Narmada slips between cliffs of white marble that rise like the walls of a giant's palace. When the moon shines, the rocks glow silver and the water whispers below.' Think it through: name the wonder, its river, and one comparison the writer uses.
st: The place named is Bhedaghat, famous for its Marble Rocks.
The river named is the Narmada.
The comparison: cliffs 'rise like the walls of a giant's palace' (a simile using 'like').
'The water whispers' is personification too.
ex.a: The Marble Rocks at Bhedaghat on the Narmada; the cliffs are compared to the walls of a giant's palace.

topics.rl: Many of these places are protected as national parks or World Heritage Sites. When we visit, we keep them clean and follow the rules so they stay wonderful.

rv.summary: 'Spectacular Wonders' takes us through amazing natural places in India and shows how to describe them vividly. Each wonder has its own state and special feature.
focus: Match each wonder to its state and feature.
Know phumdis, Keibul Lamjao and the sangai deer.
Find comparisons in a description of a wonder.
remember: Living root bridges (Meghalaya); Loktak Lake with phumdis and Keibul Lamjao, the only floating national park in the world (Manipur).
Lonar Lake (Maharashtra): a crater formed when a meteorite struck the Earth. Great Rann of Kutch (Gujarat): a vast white salt desert.
Valley of Flowers (Uttarakhand); Sundarbans (West Bengal): mangroves, Royal Bengal tiger; Marble Rocks at Bhedaghat on the Narmada (Madhya Pradesh).
traps: Don't assume every lake is formed by a river or dam; Lonar was formed by a meteorite.
Root bridges are grown, not built.
'Spectacular' (amazing to look at) is not 'spectator' (a person who watches).

topics.t: Descriptive writing: painting with words
topics.h: 'The waterfall was nice' or 'The waterfall thundered down like a river of milk'? Which one can you see and hear?
p: Descriptive writing helps the reader see, hear, smell, touch and taste a place. Use all five senses.
Choose vivid, precise words: 'roared' instead of 'made a noise', 'emerald' instead of 'green', 'tiny' instead of 'small'.
Similes (like/as), metaphors and personification make descriptions memorable: 'The lake was a mirror for the sky.'
Show, don't tell: instead of 'It was cold', write 'Our breath made little clouds and our fingers went numb.'
Organise the description: from near to far, top to bottom, or the order in which you saw things.

ex.q: Think it through: Improve this sentence with sensory details: 'The waterfall was big and nice.'
st: Sight: what does it look like? White water pouring down like milk.
Sound: what can you hear? It thunders.
Touch: what do you feel? Cool spray on your face.
Combine them into one vivid sentence.
ex.a: The waterfall thundered down the cliff like a river of milk, and its cool spray tickled our faces.

topics.rl: Travel blogs, tourism brochures and your own holiday diary all use descriptive writing to make readers wish they were there.

rv.summary: Descriptive writing helps the reader see, hear, smell, touch and taste a place. Use vivid, precise words, figures of speech, 'show, don't tell', and a clear order.
focus: Use details for all five senses.
Replace general words with vivid, precise ones.
Show, don't tell, and organise the description.
remember: Show, don't tell: instead of 'It was cold', write 'Our breath made little clouds and our fingers went numb.'
Organise from near to far, top to bottom, or in the order you saw things.
traps: Don't use general words like 'nice' or 'big'; choose precise ones like 'massive'.
Don't call every comparison a simile: 'The lake was a mirror for the sky' is a metaphor.
Don't describe in a random order; plan it.

topics.t: Prepositions of place and direction
topics.h: Does a boat sail across the lake, through the lake or along the lake? One little word changes the whole picture!
p: Prepositions show the position or movement of something in relation to something else.

across = from one side to the other of a surface (across the river); through = from one end to the other inside something (through the tunnel, through the forest); along = following the length of something (along the beach).
in = inside (in the box); into = movement to the inside (jumped into the lake). on = resting on a surface; onto = movement to a surface.
between = with two things on either side; among = surrounded by many (among the trees).
beside = next to (sat beside the lake); besides = in addition to (Besides tigers, the Sundarbans has crocodiles).

ex.q: Think it through: Choose the right prepositions: 'The train went ___ (through/across) a long tunnel and then ran ___ (along/among) the river for an hour.'
st: A tunnel is something you go inside from one end to the other: through.
Following the length of a river: along.
'Among' needs many things around you, not one river.
ex.a: through; along

topics.rl: Giving directions uses prepositions: 'Walk along the road, go across the bridge and the shop is beside the post office.'

rv.summary: Prepositions show the position or movement of something in relation to something else. Learn pairs that are easily confused: across/through, in/into, on/onto, between/among, beside/besides.
focus: Choose across, through or along from the meaning.
Use into and onto for movement.
Tell between/among and beside/besides apart.
remember: across = from one side to the other of a surface; through = from one end to the other inside something; along = following the length of something.
in = inside; into = movement to the inside; on = resting on a surface; onto = movement to a surface.
between = two things on either side; among = surrounded by many. beside = next to; besides = in addition to.
traps: Don't confuse 'across' with 'through'.
Don't use 'among' for two people; use 'between'.
Don't confuse 'beside' (next to) with 'besides' (in addition to).

topics.t: Ruskin Bond and his world of hills
topics.h: Imagine a writer who looks out of his window at the mountains every morning and turns what he sees into stories. Meet Ruskin Bond!
p: 'The Cherry Tree' is a story by Ruskin Bond about a boy who plants a cherry seed and patiently watches it grow through the seasons and the years.
Ruskin Bond is an Indian author, born on 19 May 1934 in Kasauli, Himachal Pradesh. He has lived for many years in Landour, Mussoorie, in Uttarakhand.
He writes about the hills, trees, birds, small-town life and children, in simple, warm language. His first novel, 'The Room on the Roof', was written when he was a teenager.
His well-known works include 'The Blue Umbrella', the Rusty stories, and 'Our Trees Still Grow in Dehra', which won the Sahitya Akademi Award. He has received the Padma Shri and the Padma Bhushan.
His stories often show that small, everyday things, like a seed or a bird, hold great joy if we notice them.

ex.q: Read this original passage: 'Tara pressed an apricot stone into the soil behind her house in Almora. For weeks nothing happened. She almost forgot it. Then one rainy morning she spotted two tiny green leaves pushing up through the earth, and she laughed out loud.' Think it through: what does Tara's laugh tell us, and what is the theme?
st: For weeks nothing happened, so Tara had to wait.
When the leaves appeared, she laughed out loud: she was delighted.
The joy came after a long wait.
So the theme is that patience is rewarded with the joy of growth.
ex.a: Her laugh shows delight; the theme is that patience brings the joy of seeing something grow.

topics.rl: Planting a seed in a pot on your balcony and checking it every day is a small lesson in patience, just like in Bond's stories.

rv.summary: 'The Cherry Tree' by Ruskin Bond is about a boy who plants a cherry seed and patiently watches it grow. Bond, born in Kasauli, Himachal Pradesh, lives in Landour, Mussoorie, and writes warmly about the hills and nature.
focus: Recall facts about Ruskin Bond: birth (19 May 1934, Kasauli), home (Landour, Mussoorie).
Know his works and awards.
Find the theme of a story about patience and growth.
remember: Ruskin Bond was born on 19 May 1934 in Kasauli, Himachal Pradesh; he lives in Landour, Mussoorie, Uttarakhand.
Works: 'The Room on the Roof', 'The Blue Umbrella', the Rusty stories, 'Our Trees Still Grow in Dehra' (Sahitya Akademi Award).
He has received the Padma Shri and the Padma Bhushan.
traps: Don't confuse where he was born (Himachal Pradesh) with where he lives (Uttarakhand).
'Malgudi Days' is by R. K. Narayan, not Ruskin Bond.
The Sahitya Akademi Award is a literary prize, not a sports award.

topics.t: Patience and growth: words of a growing tree
topics.h: A tree does not grow when you shout at it. It grows a little every day while you wait. What words describe that journey?
p: A tree's life: a seed germinates (sprouts), becomes a seedling, then a sapling (a young tree), then a grown tree that flowers and bears fruit.
Growth words: bud (an unopened flower or leaf), blossom (flowers of a fruit tree), bloom (to flower), wither (to dry up and shrink), prune (to cut off extra branches).
Patience is the ability to wait calmly. Patient (adjective) → patience (noun) → patiently (adverb). The opposite is impatient/impatience.
Words related to patience: perseverance (keeping on trying), endurance (bearing difficulty). Proverb: 'Rome was not built in a day.'
Growth stories teach that care, time and hope together make things grow, whether it is a tree or a skill.

ex.q: Think it through: Put the life of a fruit tree in order: sapling, seed, fruit, seedling, flowers.
st: Everything begins with a seed.
The seed sprouts into a seedling.
The seedling grows into a sapling, a young tree.
The grown tree flowers.
The flowers turn into fruit.
ex.a: seed → seedling → sapling → flowers → fruit

topics.rl: Learning to play the tabla, ride a bicycle or speak a new language also grows slowly, one small step at a time.

rv.summary: A tree grows from seed to seedling to sapling to a grown tree that flowers and bears fruit. Patience, care, time and hope make things grow, whether a tree or a skill.
focus: Order the stages of a tree's life.
Know growth words: bud, blossom, bloom, wither, prune, germinate.
Use the patience word family and related words.
remember: seed → seedling → sapling (a young tree) → grown tree → flowers → fruit.
patient (adjective) → patience (noun) → patiently (adverb); opposite: impatient/impatience.
perseverance (keeping on trying), endurance (bearing difficulty); 'Rome was not built in a day.'
traps: A sapling is a young tree, not a seed or seedling.
Don't use the adjective where an adverb is needed: 'waited patiently'.
Don't use the wrong prefix: the opposite of 'patience' is 'impatience'.

topics.t: Time and growth: present perfect with since and for
topics.h: 'The tree grew' is finished. 'The tree has grown' connects the past to now. One small helping verb, a big difference!
p: The present perfect tense = has/have + past participle: The tree has grown taller. We have planted ten saplings.
Use it for actions in the past whose result matters now, or for actions that began in the past and continue until now.
Use 'for' with a period of time (for three years, for two weeks) and 'since' with a point in time (since 2022, since Monday, since morning).
Do not use the present perfect with a finished past time like 'yesterday' or 'last year'. Say 'I planted it last year', not 'I have planted it last year'.
Present perfect continuous (has/have been + verb-ing) stresses that an action is still going on: It has been raining since morning.

ex.q: Think it through: Fill in with 'since' or 'for': 'Rohan has watered the cherry tree every day ___ June. He has cared for it ___ four months.'
st: June is a point in time, so use 'since'.
Four months is a length of time, so use 'for'.
ex.a: since June; for four months

topics.rl: We use this tense to share news: 'I have finished my project!' 'Our school has won the trophy!'

rv.summary: The present perfect (has/have + past participle) is for past actions whose result matters now, or actions that began in the past and continue. Use 'for' with a period of time and 'since' with a point in time.
focus: Form the present perfect and present perfect continuous.
Choose 'since' or 'for' correctly.
Avoid the present perfect with a finished past time.
remember: Present perfect = has/have + past participle: The tree has grown taller.
for + period (for three years); since + point in time (since 2022, since Monday).
Present perfect continuous: has/have been + verb-ing: It has been raining since morning.
traps: Don't use the present perfect with 'yesterday' or 'last year': 'I planted it last year'.
Don't mix up 'for' (period) and 'since' (point in time).
Don't use 'grew' after 'has'; use 'grown'.

topics.t: A harvest poem: praise, personification and festivals
topics.h: When fields turn gold, villages across India sing, dance and say thank you. A harvest poem joins that song.
p: 'Harvest Hymn' is a poem that celebrates the harvest and gives thanks to nature and to farmers' hard work.
A hymn is a song of praise. A harvest hymn praises the earth, rain and sun that help crops grow, and the people who grow them.
Personification gives human actions to non-human things: 'The golden fields bow low to greet the sun.' Fields cannot really bow, but the image shows heavy, ripe crops bending.
India celebrates harvest festivals in many regions: Pongal in Tamil Nadu, Lohri and Baisakhi in Punjab, Bihu in Assam, Onam in Kerala, and Makar Sankranti in many states.
Harvest poems often use warm, bright imagery (gold, glowing, ripe) and a joyful, grateful tone.

ex.q: Read this original poem: 'Golden fields bow low to greet the sun, / The sickles sing: the reaping has begun! / Rain gave its silver, soil gave its might, / Now every grain glows warm and bright.' Think it through: find two examples of personification and say what the tone is.
st: Fields 'bow low to greet the sun': bowing and greeting are human actions.
Sickles 'sing': singing is a human action, given to a tool.
Words like golden, glows, warm and bright, and the exclamation, sound happy.
Rain and soil are thanked for what they 'gave', so the poem is grateful too.
ex.a: Personification: the fields bow and greet; the sickles sing. The tone is joyful and grateful.

topics.rl: At Pongal, families cook the new rice in milk until it boils over, and at Lohri people gather around a bonfire to celebrate the season. Harvest time is thanksgiving time.

rv.summary: 'Harvest Hymn' celebrates the harvest and gives thanks to nature and to farmers' hard work. A hymn is a song of praise, and harvest poems use personification, bright imagery and a joyful, grateful tone.
focus: Explain what a hymn and a harvest hymn are.
Spot personification and describe the tone.
Match harvest festivals to their regions.
remember: A hymn is a song of praise.
Pongal (Tamil Nadu), Lohri and Baisakhi (Punjab), Bihu (Assam), Onam (Kerala), Makar Sankranti (many states).
Reaping means cutting and gathering ripe crops.
traps: Don't call every poetic image a simile; 'fields bow low' is personification.
Don't confuse reaping (harvest) with sowing (planting).
Bihu is a festival of Assam, not Bihar.

topics.t: Farmers and nature: crops, seasons and farm words
topics.h: Rice loves the monsoon and wheat loves the winter. A farmer reads the seasons like a book!
p: Kharif crops are sown at the start of the monsoon (around June-July) and harvested around September-October: rice, maize, cotton, jowar, bajra.
Rabi crops are sown in winter (around October-November) and harvested in spring (around March-April): wheat, gram, mustard, barley, peas.

Farm work follows an order: ploughing (loosening the soil), sowing (planting seeds), irrigation (watering), weeding (removing unwanted plants), harvesting (cutting the crop), threshing (separating grain from stalks).
Collective nouns for farm and nature: a herd of cattle, a flock of birds, a swarm of locusts, a sheaf of wheat, a bunch of bananas.
Farmers depend on nature (rain, sunlight, healthy soil), so they care for it by saving water and keeping soil fertile.

ex.q: Think it through: Ramesh sows seeds in June when the rains start, and harvests in October. Is his crop kharif or rabi, and which crop could it be: wheat or rice?
st: Sown with the monsoon in June and harvested in October: that is the kharif season.
Rice is a kharif crop; wheat is a rabi crop.
So the crop is kharif, most likely rice.
ex.a: Kharif; rice

topics.rl: The roti you eat is usually made from wheat, a rabi crop, and the rice in your plate is usually a kharif crop.

rv.summary: Kharif crops are sown at the start of the monsoon and rabi crops in winter. Farm work follows an order from ploughing to threshing, and farmers depend on and care for nature.
focus: Tell kharif and rabi crops apart with their seasons.
Put the steps of farm work in order.
Use the right collective nouns.
remember: Kharif: sown around June-July, harvested around September-October: rice, maize, cotton, jowar, bajra.
Rabi: sown around October-November, harvested around March-April: wheat, gram, mustard, barley, peas.
ploughing → sowing → irrigation → weeding → harvesting → threshing.
a herd of cattle, a flock of birds, a swarm of locusts, a sheaf of wheat, a bunch of bananas.
traps: Don't mix up kharif and rabi: wheat is rabi, rice is kharif.
Don't confuse threshing (separating grain from stalks) with ploughing.
Don't use 'flock' for cattle; it is a herd.

topics.t: Rain and farming: the monsoon story
topics.h: In June, millions of eyes across India look up at the sky together. They are all waiting for one guest: the monsoon!
p: 'Waiting for the Rain' is about how farming families wait for the rains, and how hope keeps them going.
The south-west monsoon usually reaches Kerala around 1 June and then spreads across India. June to September is the main monsoon season and brings most of India's yearly rainfall.
Kharif crops like rice depend on monsoon rain. If the rain is late or too little, there may be a drought (a long period with too little rain); too much rain can cause floods.
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) forecasts the weather. Rainfall is measured with a rain gauge, in millimetres.
Rain words: drizzle (light rain), downpour (very heavy rain), parched (very dry), humid (damp, sticky air), petrichor (the earthy smell when rain falls on dry ground).

ex.q: Read this original passage: 'Every evening, Baba stood at the edge of the cracked field and studied the sky. The seeds waited in their sacks. One night, a cool wind rattled the tin roof, and the smell of wet earth drifted in. Baba smiled for the first time in weeks.' Think it through: why did Baba smile?
st: The field was cracked, so it was very dry and the family needed rain.
The seeds were waiting in sacks: sowing needs rain.
A cool wind and the smell of wet earth are signs that rain has come or is coming.
So Baba smiled because the rain he was hoping for had arrived.
ex.a: He smiled because the cool wind and the smell of wet earth showed that the rain was finally coming, so he could sow his seeds.

topics.rl: Every year news channels report when the monsoon reaches Kerala, and farmers, schools and cities plan around the rains.

rv.summary: 'Waiting for the Rain' is about farming families waiting for the rains, kept going by hope. The south-west monsoon usually reaches Kerala around 1 June, and too little rain can cause drought.
focus: Infer feelings and events from clues in a passage.
Recall monsoon facts: Kerala around 1 June; June to September is the main season.
Know rain words and how rain is measured.
remember: Drought: a long period with too little rain.
Rainfall is measured with a rain gauge, in millimetres; the IMD forecasts the weather.
drizzle (light rain), downpour (very heavy rain), parched (very dry), humid (damp, sticky air), petrichor (earthy smell of rain on dry ground).
traps: Don't confuse drought with flood.
Don't miss the meaning of 'for the first time in weeks': he had been worried.
Don't focus on only one clue; the cool wind and smell of wet earth together suggest rain.

topics.t: Hope: feeling words, suffixes and idioms
topics.h: Even when the sky stays empty, a farmer keeps a sack of seeds ready. That is hope, and English has many ways to say it!
p: Hope is a feeling that something good will happen. Synonyms: optimism, expectation, faith. Antonyms: despair, hopelessness.
Suffixes change word meaning: -ful means 'full of' (hopeful, thankful, careful) and -less means 'without' (hopeless, careless, fearless, restless).
Word family: hope (noun/verb), hopeful (adjective), hopefully (adverb), hopeless (adjective), hopelessness (noun).

Idioms of hope: 'every cloud has a silver lining' (something good comes from bad times), 'light at the end of the tunnel' (a sign that a hard time is ending), 'keep your fingers crossed' (hope for luck), 'hope against hope' (keep hoping when chances are small).
Writers show hope through images of light, dawn, green shoots and clouds gathering.

ex.q: Think it through: Read this original passage: 'Three weeks passed without rain. Many neighbours sold their bullocks. But Amma still cleaned the seed sacks every morning and said, "The clouds will come."' Which word best describes Amma: hopeful or hopeless?
st: Many neighbours gave up and sold their bullocks.
Amma still prepared the seeds every morning.
She said, 'The clouds will come.' She believed good things would happen.
So she was hopeful, not hopeless.
ex.a: Hopeful

topics.rl: Before a big match, fans keep their fingers crossed. After a bad test, a teacher reminds you there is light at the end of the tunnel.

rv.summary: Hope is a feeling that something good will happen, and its opposite is despair. We learn the suffixes -ful and -less, the hope word family and idioms of hope.
focus: Know synonyms and antonyms of hope.
Use -ful (full of) and -less (without) correctly.
Know the meanings of idioms of hope.
remember: -ful means 'full of' (hopeful, thankful, careful); -less means 'without' (hopeless, careless, fearless, restless).
hope (noun/verb), hopeful (adjective), hopefully (adverb), hopeless (adjective), hopelessness (noun).
'Every cloud has a silver lining' (good comes from bad times); 'light at the end of the tunnel' (a hard time is ending).
traps: Don't confuse -less with -ful: restless is not restful.
Don't use the adverb after 'are': 'We are hopeful'.
Don't read an idiom word for word.

topics.t: Talking about the future: will, going to, hope and wish
topics.h: 'It will rain', 'It's going to rain', 'I hope it rains', 'I wish it would rain.' Four ways to talk about tomorrow!
p: 'Will' + base verb is used for predictions, promises and quick decisions: I think it will rain tomorrow. I'll help you carry the sacks.
'Be going to' + base verb is used for plans already made and for predictions based on what we can see now: We are going to sow rice next week. Look at those black clouds! It is going to rain.
The present continuous can show fixed future arrangements: We are leaving for the village on Saturday.
'Hope' is used for things that are possible: I hope it rains tomorrow. I hope you will come.
'Wish' is used for things that are unlikely or impossible now, often with a past form: I wish I could fly. I wish it were not so hot.

ex.q: Think it through: Choose 'will' or 'going to': (a) 'Look at that sky! It ___ rain.' (b) 'Don't worry, I ___ water your plants while you are away.'
st: In (a) we can see dark clouds now, so it is a prediction from present evidence: is going to.
In (b) the speaker is making a promise just now: will.
Check: 'It is going to rain' and 'I will water your plants'.
ex.a: (a) is going to; (b) will

topics.rl: Weather reports say 'It will rain in Mumbai tomorrow', and friends say 'We're going to visit Nani this summer'.

rv.summary: We talk about the future with 'will' (predictions, promises, quick decisions), 'be going to' (plans and predictions from present evidence) and the present continuous (fixed arrangements). 'Hope' is for possible things and 'wish' for unlikely or impossible ones.
focus: Choose 'will' or 'going to' from the situation.
Use the present continuous for fixed arrangements.
Tell 'hope' from 'wish'.
remember: 'Will' + base verb: predictions, promises, quick decisions.
'Be going to' + base verb: plans already made, predictions from what we can see now.
'Hope' for possible things: I hope it rains tomorrow. 'Wish' for unlikely or impossible things: I wish I could fly.
traps: Don't add -s, -ing or 'to' after 'will': 'She will go'.
Don't use 'will' for a prediction based on what you can see now; use 'going to'.
Don't use 'hope' for impossible wishes.

topics.t: Arthur C. Clarke and life on a space station
topics.h: Can a tiny bird be useful hundreds of kilometres above the Earth? A famous science fiction writer thought so!
p: 'Feathered Friend' is a science fiction story by Arthur C. Clarke in which a small pet bird on a space station turns out to matter far more than anyone expected.

Arthur C. Clarke (1917-2008) was a British writer of science fiction who lived in Sri Lanka from 1956 until his death. In 1945 he wrote about using satellites in space to send signals around the world.
In the past, miners took canaries into coal mines. These birds react to dangerous gases like carbon monoxide sooner than people do, so a canary in trouble warned miners to get out.
On a space station, astronauts float because they are in free fall around the Earth (often called weightlessness or microgravity). Air, water and food must be carried up or recycled.
The International Space Station orbits about 400 km above the Earth and goes around it roughly every 90 minutes.

ex.q: Read this original passage: 'On Moon Base Chandra, Ravi grew tomatoes under bright lamps. One morning every plant was drooping, though he had watered them the night before. He checked the water recycler and found it had stopped working.' Think it through: how did the plants help Ravi?
st: Ravi had watered the plants, so drooping was unexpected.
The drooping was a warning sign that something was wrong.
Ravi checked the water recycler and found the fault.
So the plants acted like an early warning system.
ex.a: The drooping plants warned Ravi that the water recycler had failed, so he could find and fix the problem.

topics.rl: Many homes today have smoke detectors and gas alarms that do the job miners' canaries once did: they warn us early about danger.

rv.summary: 'Feathered Friend' is a science fiction story by Arthur C. Clarke in which a small pet bird on a space station turns out to matter far more than anyone expected. The lesson also explains how canaries once warned coal miners of dangerous gases.
focus: Recall facts about Arthur C. Clarke (1917-2008), who lived in Sri Lanka from 1956.
Explain why miners took canaries into coal mines.
Know basic facts about life on a space station.
remember: Canaries react to dangerous gases like carbon monoxide sooner than people do, so they warned miners to get out.
Astronauts float because they are in free fall around the Earth (weightlessness or microgravity).
The ISS orbits about 400 km above the Earth, roughly every 90 minutes.
traps: Canaries in mines were not kept just as pets; they were an early warning.
Don't pick oxygen; the dangerous gas was carbon monoxide.
Don't ignore the contrast word 'though' when reading for surprise.

topics.t: Science fiction: imagining tomorrow with science
topics.h: A robot that cooks dosa, a bus to Mars, a phone that translates birdsong. If it uses science to imagine the future, it's science fiction!
p: Science fiction (sci-fi) is imaginative writing based on science and technology. It asks 'What if...?' about the future, space, inventions or other worlds.
Sci-fi is different from fantasy: fantasy uses magic, while sci-fi tries to explain things through science, even when the science is imagined.
Common features: future or space settings, new inventions, scientists or astronauts as characters, and problems solved by reasoning.
Some sci-fi ideas later came true, such as communication satellites, video calls and robots.

India has its own sci-fi tradition, including Satyajit Ray's stories about the inventor Professor Shonku. India's real space journey includes Rakesh Sharma, the first Indian in space (1984), and Chandrayaan-3, which landed near the Moon's south pole on 23 August 2023.

ex.q: Think it through: Is this science fiction or fantasy? 'In 2090, Asha boarded a solar-powered shuttle to a farm on Mars, where robots grew wheat inside glass domes.'
st: Look at the setting: the future (2090) and Mars.
Look at the technology: a solar-powered shuttle, robots, glass domes.
Is there any magic? No, everything is explained by technology.
So it is science fiction.
ex.a: Science fiction

topics.rl: Space missions by ISRO, like Chandrayaan and the Gaganyaan human spaceflight programme, show how yesterday's sci-fi dreams become today's science.

rv.summary: Science fiction is imaginative writing based on science and technology that asks 'What if...?' about the future, space or inventions. Unlike fantasy, which uses magic, sci-fi explains things through science.
focus: Tell science fiction from fantasy.
Know common sci-fi features and ideas that came true.
Recall India's sci-fi and space facts.
remember: Sci-fi explains events through science (even imagined); fantasy uses magic.
Rakesh Sharma was the first Indian in space (1984).
Chandrayaan-3 landed near the Moon's south pole on 23 August 2023.
Professor Shonku is Satyajit Ray's inventor; Feluda is his detective.
traps: Don't confuse sci-fi with fantasy; magic or talking animals make it fantasy.
Sci-fi does not have to be true.
Kalpana Chawla flew later (1997); the first Indian in space was Rakesh Sharma.

topics.t: Science words: roots and prefixes
topics.h: An 'astronaut' is a star sailor! Many science words hide old Greek and Latin roots. Crack the code and you can guess new words!
p: Many science words are built from roots and prefixes that come from Greek or Latin.
tele = far (telephone, telescope, television); micro = very small (microscope, microphone); astro/astr = star (astronaut, astronomy).
bio = life (biology, biography); geo = earth (geography, geology); photo = light (photograph, photosynthesis); hydro = water (hydropower).
scope = look at (telescope, microscope); graph = write or draw (autograph, photograph); phone = sound (telephone, microphone); naut = sailor (astronaut).
logy = study of (biology, geology, zoology). So geology is the study of the earth.

ex.q: Think it through: Use roots to work out what a 'microscope' does and what 'biology' means.
st: micro = very small; scope = look at. A microscope helps you look at very small things.
bio = life; logy = study of. Biology is the study of living things.
ex.a: A microscope is for looking at very small things; biology is the study of life.

topics.rl: When you see a new word in science class, like 'thermometer' (therm = heat, meter = measure), roots help you guess its meaning.

rv.summary: Many science words are built from Greek or Latin roots and prefixes. Knowing the roots helps you work out what a new word means.
focus: Know the meanings of common science roots.
Split a word into roots to find its meaning.
Tell similar words apart, like biology and biography.
remember: tele = far; micro = very small; astro = star; bio = life; geo = earth; photo = light; hydro = water.
scope = look at; graph = write or draw; phone = sound; naut = sailor; logy = study of.
therm = heat, meter = measure: thermometer.
traps: Don't confuse 'biology' (study of life) with 'biography' (written life story).
'Phone' as a root means sound, not a mobile phone.
'Photo' means light, not only pictures.

topics.t: A poem on observing closely: imagery and looking words
topics.h: Hold a magnifying glass over an ordinary leaf, and suddenly it looks like a map of rivers! Close looking turns the ordinary into the amazing.
p: 'Magnifying Glass' is a poem about looking closely at small things and discovering wonder in them.
A magnifying glass is a convex lens (thicker in the middle) that makes things look bigger than they are.
Imagery means word pictures that appeal to the senses. Poets use imagery and metaphors to show what close looking reveals: 'a beetle's back becomes a shining shield'.

Looking words have different shades of meaning: observe and examine (look carefully), peer (look closely, as if it is hard to see), inspect (check for details or faults), glance and glimpse (look quickly or briefly).
Close observation is the first step of science and of good writing: notice details, colours, shapes, patterns and changes.

ex.q: Read this original poem: 'Through my glass a beetle's back / Becomes a shining shield of black; / A leaf turns into a map of streams, / A drop of dew holds rainbow gleams.' Think it through: what does the leaf become, and why is that a good image?
st: The poem says the leaf 'turns into a map of streams'.
Under a magnifying glass, the veins of a leaf look like rivers branching on a map.
This is a metaphor: it compares the leaf directly to a map.
It helps us see the leaf's tiny veins in a new way.
ex.a: The leaf becomes 'a map of streams', because its veins look like branching rivers when magnified.

topics.rl: Scientists use magnifying lenses and microscopes, jewellers check gems with a small lens, and you can watch ants or study a flower's parts in your garden.

rv.summary: 'Magnifying Glass' is a poem about looking closely at small things and discovering wonder in them. It uses imagery and metaphors, and we learn looking words with different shades of meaning.
focus: Explain the poem's main message.
Find metaphors and imagery in the lines.
Choose the right looking word.
remember: A magnifying glass is a convex lens (thicker in the middle) that makes things look bigger.
Imagery means word pictures that appeal to the senses.
observe/examine (look carefully), peer (look closely, as if hard to see), inspect (check for details or faults), glance/glimpse (look quickly).
traps: Don't confuse convex with concave.
Don't call it a simile without 'like' or 'as': 'A leaf turns into a map of streams' is a metaphor.
Imagery does not mean printed images.

topics.t: Curiosity: asking good questions and question tags
topics.h: Why is the sky blue? How do ants find sugar? Every great discovery begins with a curious question!
p: Curiosity means a strong wish to know or learn. Curious (adjective) → curiosity (noun). Note the spelling: curiosity, not 'curiousity'.
Wh-questions ask for information: what, where, when, why, who, which, whose, how. 'Why do leaves change colour?'
Yes/no questions begin with a helping verb: Is, Are, Do, Does, Did, Can, Have. 'Does the lens make things bigger?'
In questions, the helping verb comes before the subject: 'Where does the beetle live?' (not 'Where the beetle lives?').

A question tag is a short question at the end of a sentence. A positive statement takes a negative tag and a negative statement takes a positive tag: 'It's a lens, isn't it?' 'You don't like spiders, do you?'

ex.q: Think it through: Turn this observation into two good questions: 'The ants walk in a line towards the sugar.'
st: A wh-question asking why: Why do the ants walk in a line?
A wh-question asking how: How do the ants find the sugar?
Check the order: helping verb 'do' comes before the subject 'the ants'.
ex.a: Why do the ants walk in a line? How do the ants find the sugar?

topics.rl: Scientists, journalists and detectives all ask good questions. In class, asking 'Why?' and 'How?' helps you understand, not just remember.

rv.summary: Curiosity is a strong wish to know or learn, and good questions come from it. We learn wh-questions, yes/no questions, correct question word order and question tags.
focus: Spell curiosity correctly.
Form questions with the helping verb before the subject.
Choose the right question tag.
remember: Curious (adjective) → curiosity (noun), not 'curiousity'.
In questions, the helping verb comes before the subject: 'Where does the beetle live?'
Positive statement → negative tag; negative statement → positive tag: 'It's a lens, isn't it?' 'You don't like spiders, do you?'
traps: Don't keep the 'u' from 'curious' in 'curiosity'.
Don't use statement word order in a question.
Don't repeat the negative in the tag; for simple past use 'did': 'didn't she?'

topics.ch: Bibha Chowdhuri: The Beam of Light that Lit the Path for Women in Indian Science
topics.t: Bibha Chowdhuri: the physicist who studied cosmic rays
topics.h: Somewhere in the night sky, there is a star named after an Indian woman scientist. Who was she?
p: The lesson tells the life story of Bibha Chowdhuri, an Indian physicist whose work lit the way for women in Indian science.
Bibha Chowdhuri was born in 1913 in Calcutta (now Kolkata). She studied physics at the University of Calcutta at a time when very few women studied science.

At the Bose Institute in Kolkata, she worked with the physicist D. M. Bose. They used photographic plates to detect tiny particles produced by cosmic rays, which are high-energy particles that reach the Earth from outer space.

She earned her PhD at the University of Manchester in England, working in the laboratory of Patrick Blackett, who won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1948. Back in India she worked at research centres such as the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research and the Physical Research Laboratory.
In 2019, the International Astronomical Union named a star 'Bibha' in her honour.

ex.q: Read this original passage: 'In the 1930s, most girls in Bengal were not encouraged to study science. Bibha chose physics anyway, sat in classrooms full of young men, and went on to study particles that come from far beyond the Earth.' Think it through: which two qualities does this passage show?
st: Girls were not encouraged, yet she chose physics: that shows courage and determination.
She went on to study particles from space: that shows curiosity and love of science.
The word 'anyway' shows that she did not let others' expectations stop her.
ex.a: Determination (she chose physics anyway) and curiosity (she studied particles from beyond the Earth).

topics.rl: When you see a girl topping a science olympiad or building a robot at a school fair, she is walking on a path that pioneers like Bibha Chowdhuri helped to open.

rv.summary: Bibha Chowdhuri, born in 1913 in Calcutta, was an Indian physicist who studied particles produced by cosmic rays and lit the way for women in Indian science. In 2019 a star was named 'Bibha' in her honour.
focus: Recall key facts: physics, Bose Institute with D. M. Bose, PhD at Manchester.
Explain what cosmic rays are.
Describe her qualities from a passage.
remember: Cosmic rays are high-energy particles that reach the Earth from outer space.
She earned her PhD at the University of Manchester, in Patrick Blackett's laboratory.
In 2019, the International Astronomical Union named a star 'Bibha' in her honour.
traps: Cosmic rays are not ordinary light.
Don't mix up the 2019 star naming with her birth year (1913).
'The Beam of Light' is a metaphor, not a simile.

topics.t: Women in Indian science: pioneers and the words to describe them
topics.h: A botanist who improved sugarcane, a 'weather woman', a 'missile woman' and an astronaut! India's women scientists have done it all.
p: Janaki Ammal was a botanist who worked on breeding better sugarcane. Asima Chatterjee was a chemist who studied medicines made from plants.
Anna Mani was a physicist and meteorologist who made instruments for measuring the weather. Kamala Sohonie was a biochemist who studied the nutrition in foods.

Kalpana Chawla, born in Karnal, Haryana, became the first woman of Indian origin to go to space, in 1997. Tessy Thomas, a scientist at DRDO, is known as the 'Missile Woman of India' for her work on the Agni missiles.
A pioneer is one of the first people to do something and so opens the way for others. Many of these women were pioneers.
Words to describe them: determined, brilliant, dedicated, inspiring, persistent. Nouns: determination, dedication, inspiration, achievement.

ex.q: Think it through: Read: 'India had to buy most weather instruments from abroad, so Anna Mani helped design and build them in India.' Choose the best adjective for her: lazy, resourceful or careless.
st: India lacked its own weather instruments.
Instead of depending on others, she helped make them in India.
A person who finds clever ways to solve problems is resourceful.
ex.a: Resourceful

topics.rl: Today women scientists lead missions at ISRO, research medicines in labs and teach science in colleges across India, building on these pioneers.

rv.summary: Many Indian women scientists were pioneers who opened the way for others. We learn who they were, their fields, and words to describe them.
focus: Match each scientist to her field and work.
Know the meaning of 'pioneer'.
Use describing adjectives and nouns correctly.
remember: Janaki Ammal: botanist (sugarcane). Asima Chatterjee: chemist (medicines from plants). Anna Mani: weather instruments. Kamala Sohonie: biochemist (nutrition in foods).
Kalpana Chawla, born in Karnal, Haryana: first woman of Indian origin in space (1997). Tessy Thomas (DRDO): 'Missile Woman of India'.
A pioneer is one of the first people to do something and so opens the way for others.
traps: Don't mix up the scientists and their fields.
Don't use an adjective where a noun is needed: 'Her dedication'.
Judge a character from the action in the sentence, e.g. resourceful.
